_note: scripts/blogs.py reads this. One entry per platform. rate is requests a second across every thread; workers the requests in flight. A platform with enabled false is skipped by `run`. robots: ignore fetches without the robots.txt check, on Alex's decision, with the reason in the note.

substack.note: The platform's sitemap index lists every publication on a substack.com subdomain with the time of its last post; the ones on their own domain come from the category leaderboards (weekly sweep at leaderboard_rate a second; a 429 from substack.com halts it and the rest is done next hour) and are polled through their archive API's ETag (a 304 when nothing changed), each about as often as it posts: custom_poll's per_post times its average gap between posts (from the oldest of its last ten stored posts to now, over their number), kept between min_hours and max_hours, then spread by up to a fifth either way. Every three hours until 2026-09-16, which was about 20,000 requests a day for some 1,200 new posts; per_post 0.5 and max_hours 24 (twice as often as it posts, Alex's choice) is about 3,400 a day, the posts found an estimated 6.5 hours after publication on average instead of 1.5 (per_post 1 and max_hours 48 would be about 1,800 requests and 13 hours). first_run_days: on the first run, only publications that posted within this many days are read; the rest are recorded for the history walk. pages_per_site caps how far an hourly run pages back for one publication (50 a page). robots.txt (one file for every subdomain) allows the sitemaps and the archive API; the API terms (substack.com/api-tos, 2026-01-08) allow discovery and analytics over public publications and forbid reselling the data as a dataset; the general terms of service have a clause against crawling or scraping any part of Substack, noted for Alex on 2026-09-13. A 429 from a publication halves the pace (a burst within ten seconds counts once; the floor is one request per eight seconds), which comes back a step for every five minutes without another; after twenty within one batch of flush_every the rest of the queue waits for next hour. Posts, fetch log and site state are written every flush_every publications. rate 0.5 since 2026-09-13 night: at one a second sustained Substack answered 429 to about one request in twenty-five from the box, at two a second to one in eight from home.

medium.note: One sitemap file per day of every post, listed in robots.txt; the file for a day appears the next morning and is touched again for a day or two, so the last `days` days' files are re-read when the index says they changed. Titles are the URL slugs. robots.txt allows the sitemaps to unnamed bots (it names the AI crawlers it turns away); the terms of service (read 2026-09-13 through the Wayback Machine, since policy.medium.com answers 403 to curl) have no clause on automated reading; the License file robots.txt points to could not be read (blocked).
